feature_name: Runtime contracts split from engine (dependency-direction gate)
feature_description: Split ResearchRunRequest, ResearchRunResult, and RunConflictError out of runtime/engine.py into a new runtime/contracts.py, and repoint the four modules that only ever needed the contracts (cli.py, runtime/batch.py, product/research.py, backtest/validation.py) so they stop transitively depending on ResearchEngine's SQLite storage (storage.recovery, storage.sqlite).
entrypoint: uv run pytest tests/unit/test_import_layering.py -k 'runtime_contracts or contract_only';uv run pytest tests/unit/runtime/test_contracts_import_isolation.py
notes: Also exercised by test_runtime_contracts_module_does_not_import_runtime_engine, test_runtime_contracts_module_does_not_transitively_depend_on_storage, and test_contract_only_consumers_do_not_transitively_reach_engine_owned_storage_modules in tests/unit/test_import_layering.py, all using grimp.build_graph per the existing Task-4 idiom, not runtime sys.modules introspection. Verified by mutation: reverting any one of the four modules' import line back to `from openalpha_cn.runtime.engine import ...` makes the direct-edge test fail. The transitive-storage check is scoped to storage.recovery/storage.sqlite specifically, not all of openalpha_cn.storage, because two of the four modules retain real, pre-existing, unrelated storage touchpoints out of this task's scope: cli.py separately needs backtest.replay.ReplayCorpus (which needs the full ResearchEngine for its `replay` subcommand), and runtime.batch has its own TYPE_CHECKING-only reference to storage.batch.SQLiteBatchTaskStore for an unrelated method parameter. runtime/__init__.py resolves ResearchEngine lazily via a module __getattr__ (PEP 562) instead of an eager top-level import, because Python always executes a package's __init__.py before any of its submodules -- an eager import there would silently reintroduce the storage dependency at real runtime for anyone merely importing runtime.contracts. A reviewer proved that guard previously had no automated backstop: grimp records function-local and eager top-level imports as the same static edge, so it cannot see whether ResearchEngine resolution actually runs at import time. That gap is now closed by tests/unit/runtime/test_contracts_import_isolation.py::test_importing_runtime_contracts_in_a_fresh_process_does_not_load_the_storage_layer, a subprocess-isolated test (launched via sys.executable, so it runs under the same interpreter/venv as the rest of the suite) that imports openalpha_cn.runtime.contracts in a brand-new Python process and asserts openalpha_cn.storage and every submodule under it are absent from that process's real sys.modules -- an in-process check would be meaningless, since pytest has already imported most of openalpha_cn, including the storage layer, by the time any test runs. Verified by mutation: temporarily making runtime/__init__.py's ResearchEngine import eager makes this test fail, naming the leaked openalpha_cn.storage, .memory, .parquet, .recovery, and .sqlite modules; restoring the lazy form makes it pass again. This is a narrow, deliberate exception to the task brief's general prohibition on runtime sys.modules checks: that prohibition targets the dependency-direction assertions above, where grimp's static analysis is the right tool; here static analysis is structurally blind to eager-vs-lazy import timing, so a runtime check is the only tool that can verify this specific property. The test deliberately does not assert bare sqlite3 absence from sys.modules: at the time this task was written, models/governance.py imported sqlite3 directly at module scope for ModelRegistry's durable usage accounting, reached from runtime.contracts via agents.base -> agents/__init__.py -> agents.model -> models.base -> models/__init__.py -> models.openai_compatible -> models.governance -- a layering exemption tracked then as baseline entry V2-P0B-011 (models.governance -> sqlite3), unrelated to ResearchEngine's lazy resolution and out of this task's scope. V2-P0B-011 has since fixed it: SQLiteModelUsageStore moved to storage/models.py and models/governance.py now declares a structural ModelUsageStore Protocol instead of importing sqlite3, so a fresh import openalpha_cn.runtime.contracts no longer pulls sqlite3 into sys.modules through this chain at all, and that baseline entry is gone (see docs/architecture/import-layering-baseline.toml). This test's own scope remains openalpha_cn.storage specifically rather than bare sqlite3, so its assertions did not change when that exemption was fixed; a fresh import openalpha_cn.runtime.contracts today (verified directly, not just inferred) no longer pulls bare sqlite3 into sys.modules at all through any chain in this project's current dependency graph, but the test still checks openalpha_cn.storage rather than widening to sqlite3, since a storage-layer regression -- not a sqlite3-importing one -- is what this test exists to catch.

Proven by the opposite mutation: temporarily narrowing both container fields to BatchTaskStore/PortfolioLedger makes mypy reject exactly those four call sites (sdk.py:202, api/app.py:435, api/app.py:450, api/app.py:508) with 'has no attribute list'/'list_events', reverted after confirming. The recover_interrupted clock divergence flagged by the task brief (api/app.py previously hardcoded datetime.now(UTC) while sdk.py used its injected self.clock) is closed by moving the single batch_store.recover_interrupted(now=clock()) call inside build_storage() itself, using whichever clock the caller supplies; sdk.py and api/app.py no longer call it at all. The F32 regression test, test_single_and_batch_endpoints_accept_the_same_serialized_evidence_payload, was confirmed red before the fix: POSTing a payload with evidence_id/content_hash present to /api/v1/research/batches returned 422 extra_forbidden on both fields while /api/v1/research/run returned 200; reverting BatchSubmitRequest.requests to a bare ResearchRunRequest reproduces that failure.

feature_name: SQLite schema migration engine (versioned, transactional, backup-and-rollback)
feature_description: Add a forward-only SQLite schema-migration engine for the shared state.sqlite3 that all seven SQLite stores share: PRAGMA user_version is the cheap, atomic current-version marker; a new schema_migrations table (version, name, applied_at) is a human-readable audit trail alongside it. Migrations are a plain, hand-ordered tuple (MIGRATIONS), sorted by version at run time, not a directory-scanning plugin system or alembic -- the runtime dependency set stays at seven packages. run_migrations() applies every pending migration inside its own BEGIN IMMEDIATE/COMMIT transaction (DDL, the audit row, and the PRAGMA user_version bump are one atomic unit); any failure rolls the whole unit back and re-raises MigrationFailedError naming the pre-migration backup, without advancing user_version. run_migrations() always backs up state.sqlite3 (via the SQLite backup API, safe under WAL) to runtime_dir/backups before applying anything pending. A baseline migration (version 1) stamps both a brand-new database and an existing, unversioned v1-shaped database (created before this task existed) at the baseline version without touching data. A demo migration (version 2, demo_add_runs_archived_at) adds a nullable runs.archived_at column, proving the executor can make a real, additive schema change to a table already holding real records while those records stay fully readable through the unmodified SQLiteRunRepository afterwards -- the acceptance proof PRD Story S88 and Testing Decision 16 require. Because migrations run before any store is constructed (the composition-root mount point in runtime/composition.py's build_storage(), per the task brief), a migration that alters a pre-existing table raises MigrationNotYetApplicable against a brand-new install where that table doesn't exist yet; the executor stops without error and retries on the next invocation, once the owning store has created the table. Two new CLI commands, 'openalpha migrate status' and 'openalpha migrate run' (with --dry-run), expose the current version, the applied/pending migration lists, and the backup path.
notes: The core proof is test_demo_migration_advances_version_and_preserves_v1_records: it builds a v1-shaped database using only the pre-existing, unmodified SQLiteRunRepository and SQLiteResearchMemory stores (one run manifest, one decision, one memory entry -- exactly as brief section 5 specifies), confirms it has no version stamp and no schema_migrations table (a real old-shaped library), runs the migration engine, and asserts: user_version advances from 0 to 2, schema_migrations records both migrations by name, runs.archived_at now exists (the real schema change happened), and all three pre-migration records are still readable byte-for-byte through the same unmodified stores. Also exercised by test_running_migrations_again_is_idempotent (a second run applies nothing and takes no new backup), test_demo_migration_is_a_sql_level_no_op_when_the_column_already_exists (covers the migration's own duplicate-column guard, independent of the framework-level already-applied guard), test_new_database_lands_on_baseline_and_defers_the_demo_migration and tests/unit/runtime/test_composition_migrations.py's two tests (proving build_storage() never crashes a brand-new install and catches the deferred migration up on the next call), and tests/integration/test_cli_migrate.py's four tests for 'migrate status', 'migrate run --dry-run', and 'migrate run'. Failure/rollback semantics are proven, not reasoned about, by test_failing_migration_rolls_back_leaves_version_unmoved_and_backup_intact: a deliberately doomed migration (version 3) runs a real ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN and then raises, inside the same BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction as the audit-row insert and the PRAGMA user_version write; the test asserts user_version is unchanged, no schema_migrations row exists for version 3, the doomed column is absent from runs (proving SQLite DDL genuinely rolled back, not just the bookkeeping), the pre-existing run record is still readable, and the pre-migration backup file still exists on disk. A standalone Python experiment (documented in the task report) independently confirmed PRAGMA user_version participates correctly in an explicit BEGIN/ROLLBACK transaction under Python 3.11's sqlite3 module, while PRAGMA journal_mode does not -- it raises OperationalError if executed inside an open transaction at all -- which is why run_migrations() never touches journal_mode itself and leaves WAL-mode setup to each store's own _initialize(), unchanged. No existing CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS statement in any of the seven stores was moved or edited; storage/migrations.py imports only sqlite3 and the standard library, so it adds no new lint-imports edge beyond the pre-existing legal runtime -> storage direction composition.py already uses.

feature_name: Migration engine hardening: CLI convergence, honest status reporting, race-safe execution, collision-free backups, and a fresh-install guard
feature_description: Closes six reviewer-confirmed Important gaps in the V2-P0B-004 migration engine (OA-OPS-021), without changing its deferral design. (1) 'openalpha migrate run' used to call run_migrations() directly, bypassing build_storage() -- it never constructed a store, so a migration deferred only because its owning table did not exist yet (the demo migration on a fresh install) stayed pending forever no matter how many times the command ran. migrate_run now goes through build_storage() -- the same composition root sdk.py/api/app.py use -- so the stores it constructs as a side effect let the next invocation's migration attempt actually converge. (2) migrate_run used to branch on 'not result.applied' alone and print 'up to date' even while read_status().pending was non-empty, contradicting 'migrate status' on the same directory in the same breath; it now checks read_status().pending after running and only ever claims completion when nothing is applied and nothing is pending, otherwise reporting the still-pending migrations by name. (3) Nothing previously forced a future migration to defer safely on a fresh, empty database -- the demo migration was safe only because it hand-wrote a table-exists check. storage/migrations.py now exposes a reusable require_table(connection, name) guard, and a structural test runs every non-baseline migration in the real MIGRATIONS registry against a genuinely empty database, asserting it raises MigrationNotYetApplicable rather than crashing -- so a Phase P4 migration that omits the check fails this test instead of crashing OpenAlphaSDK.__init__/create_app() for every fresh install. (4) '.bak' backup files (SQLite binary dumps, just like '.sqlite3'/'.db'/'.duckdb') were missing from scripts/verify_publication.py's BLOCKED_SUFFIXES, so an untracked '.bak' that escaped .gitignore (e.g. under a custom --runtime-dir) would publish clean; '.bak' is now blocked like its siblings. (5) The pre-migration backup filename ({name}.v{version}.{timestamp}.bak, second precision) had no collision check, so two backups at the same version within the same second silently overwrote each other; _take_backup now claims its filename with os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL (atomic at the OS level, not an exists-then-create race) and falls back to a numeric suffix on collision. (6) run_migrations()'s per-migration loop computed its pending list once, before acquiring any lock, so two concurrent callers on the same runtime_dir (e.g. the API and the CLI) could both decide the same migration was pending; the loser's BEGIN IMMEDIATE would then succeed after the winner committed, replay migration.apply(), and hit a primary-key collision on its own schema_migrations insert -- reported as a genuine MigrationFailedError even though the database had converged correctly. Each loop iteration now re-reads PRAGMA user_version immediately after acquiring the write lock and skips a migration a concurrent winner already committed, instead of replaying it.
notes: test_concurrent_run_migrations_does_not_report_a_false_failure races two real, separate OS processes (multiprocessing's spawn start method launches a fresh interpreter, not a thread) against the same fresh database with a deliberately slow migration to force the BEGIN IMMEDIATE contention deterministically (the reviewer's own natural-timing reproduction was 1-in-5); it is confirmed RED against the pre-fix executor (fails 3/3 runs with a false MigrationFailedError) and GREEN against the fix (5/5 runs). test_every_non_baseline_migration_defers_gracefully_on_a_fresh_empty_database is the Finding 1c structural guard: it independently reproduces a bare sqlite3.OperationalError crash when tried against a hand-rolled careless migration missing require_table(), proving the guard has teeth. test_take_backup_does_not_overwrite_an_existing_backup_at_the_same_timestamp is RED against the pre-fix naive filename (both backups collide on the same path) and GREEN against the O_CREAT|O_EXCL fix. test_migrate_run_converges_after_it_constructs_stores_then_reports_up_to_date (tests/integration/test_cli_migrate.py) replaces test_migrate_run_a_second_time_reports_up_to_date, which asserted the Finding 1b lie as correct behaviour; the new test is RED against the pre-fix CLI (first assertion fails: the CLI still claims 'up to date' while genuinely stuck) and GREEN against the fix, and additionally proves Finding 1a's convergence end to end through the real CLI (a second invocation on the same fresh runtime_dir actually applies the demo migration, and only a third, truly-idle invocation reports 'up to date'). test_publication_gate_blocks_sqlite_backup_files pins '.bak' in BLOCKED_SUFFIXES directly; separately verified end to end by placing an untracked reviewer_repro.bak at the repo root and confirming scripts/verify_publication.py now reports it blocked (not committed; a throwaway manual repro).

feature_name: Version-dispatched contract reads: row-content schema upgrade mechanism
feature_description: Version-dispatched reads for stored contract payloads, closing the read-side half of V2-P0B-004/OA-OPS-021's table-migration story: eight contracts carry a literal schema_version field (signal.py:17, run.py:49, decision.py:29, validation.py:28, evidence.py:30, providers/base.py:85,115, storage/recovery.py:24) combined with extra="forbid", so Model.model_validate_json(row) hard-fails the moment a row's schema_version is one this build's Literal does not carry -- in either direction, upgraded code reading an old row or old code reading a row written by a newer build. domain/versioning.py adds ContractVersions[T], a plain per-contract registry (mirroring storage/migrations.py's Migration dataclass, not a versioning framework) mapping every schema_version this build knows to its model plus an upgrade chain to the current version, and read_versioned(), which parses raw JSON with the stdlib json module -- deliberately not pydantic -- to read schema_version out of a plain dict before any model sees the payload, then dispatches, validates at the payload's own version (so a genuinely malformed row still raises its own model's ValidationError, never confused with a version mismatch), and walks the upgrade chain to current_version. An unregistered schema_version raises UnknownSchemaVersionError naming the contract, the payload's version, and every version this build supports -- explicit failure instead of silent misreading, per the brief. All 15 of storage/'s Model.model_validate_json(row[0]) call sites (portfolio.py x2, product.py x3, batch.py x3, sqlite.py x4, memory.py x2, recovery.py x1) now go through read_versioned(); the 7 storage models with no schema_version field (PortfolioTransition, WatchlistEntry, ResearchReport, BatchResearchTask, BatchProgressEvent, CheckpointRecord, MemoryEntry) get a single_version() registry keyed on None -- the value payload.get('schema_version') naturally returns when the key is absent -- so every stored-row read in this package goes through one mechanism, and giving one of these models a real schema_version later is a registry edit at its own definition, not a call-site audit. No v2 of any real contract is created (that is Phase P4's job); the upgrade chain itself is proven end to end with a synthetic, test-only demo-widget v1->v2 contract in tests/unit/domain/test_versioning.py, exactly as storage/migrations.py's demo migration proved the table-migration engine. test_schema_export.py's line-19 assertion, which hardcoded checked_in["properties"]["schema_version"]["const"].endswith("/v1") and would fail by design the moment any contract is upversioned, now compares against each contract's ContractVersions.current_version instead; it still catches an unregenerated schema file via the pre-existing deep checked_in == schema comparison (verified by a manual repro: mutating a checked-in schema's schema_version const away from the runtime model's value reproduces the failure), and additionally now catches a registry whose current_version was never bumped to match a correctly regenerated schema file. A concluded, documented finding for Phase P4: stable_model_id (domain/_identity.py) hashes model_dump(mode='json', exclude_computed_fields=True), and schema_version is a real (non-computed) field, so it participates in the hash for the four contracts whose computed id is built with stable_model_id -- SignalFrame.signal_id, DecisionLedger.decision_id, ValidationResult.validation_id, ProviderRecord.record_id. An upcast that bumps schema_version therefore changes the recomputed id even when every other field is identical, while the row's own stored primary key was computed and written at the old version -- a real migration cutting v2 of any of these four contracts must treat that identity shift as a Task-11-style, auditable, atomic migration (rewriting the stored key), not a transparent read-time illusion. EvidenceSnapshot.evidence_id is the contrasting safe pattern: it is hand-derived from (subject, kind, source_id, timeline.available_time, content_hash) and deliberately excludes schema_version.
notes: test_read_versioned_does_not_require_new_v2_fields_when_reading_a_v1_payload is the acceptance test because it is the brief's central subtlety made concrete: it first proves _DemoWidgetV2.model_validate_json(v1_raw) raises pydantic.ValidationError on its own (a required v2-only field is missing), then proves read_versioned(raw) succeeds anyway by reading schema_version out of the raw dict, dispatching to _DemoWidgetV1, and upgrading -- so a try/except around model_validate_json could not have produced this result. test_read_versioned_lets_a_genuine_validation_error_propagate_unchanged is the companion proof that a malformed-but-correctly-versioned payload still raises ValidationError, not UnknownSchemaVersionError, so the two failure modes stay distinguishable. Confirmed RED before domain/versioning.py existed: importing it failed with ModuleNotFoundError; confirmed RED again for the storage wiring before the registries existed: ImportError on DECISION_LEDGER_VERSIONS. tests/integration/storage/test_versioned_reads.py proves the hard constraint end to end against real SQLite databases built through today's normal write paths: test_sqlite_run_repository_reads_existing_records_field_for_field and test_sqlite_recovery_store_reads_existing_records_field_for_field append via SQLiteRunRepository/SQLiteRecoveryStore then assert the read_versioned()-routed get_run/get_decision/get_decision_for_run/list_checkpoints/get results equal the originally constructed objects field for field; test_sqlite_run_repository_get_run_fails_loudly_on_an_unknown_schema_version, ..._get_decision_fails_loudly_..., and test_sqlite_recovery_store_get_fails_loudly_on_an_unknown_schema_version hand-insert a row carrying schema_version='<contract>/v2' directly via sqlite3 (bypassing the pydantic model entirely) and assert UnknownSchemaVersionError names the contract, the found version, and the supported set -- reproducing, with a real database, the 'old code meets a newer row' scenario the brief calls out. All pre-existing 205 tests plus these 14 new ones (219 total) pass; uv run mypy src scripts, ruff check, ruff format --check, and lint-imports (4 contracts kept, 0 broken, unchanged from baseline) are all clean; coverage is 88.30%, above the 80% floor. Write paths were not touched -- every store still serializes via model_dump_json() at the model's own current schema_version; only the 15 read call sites changed.

feature_name: Typed OPENALPHA_* config object and in-process .env loading
feature_description: Add a single typed OPENALPHA_* config object (OpenAlphaConfig, pydantic-settings) replacing 9 scattered os.getenv/os.environ call sites in api/app.py and cli.py, plus in-process .env loading for the openalpha CLI (load_dotenv(), invoked once by cli.py#main, never by module import or SDK construction). Real environment variables always win over the same key in .env, which wins over compiled-in defaults. Fixes: the import-time crash from an unguarded int(os.getenv('OPENALPHA_MAX_REQUEST_BYTES')) (now a named ConfigError, never a bare traceback); OPENALPHA_WEB_DIR being read but undeclared in .env.example (now declared); OPENALPHA_HOST/OPENALPHA_PORT being dead variables for 'openalpha serve' (now real precedence: --host/--port > env/.env > default); Dockerfile's CMD hardcoding --host/--port and silently shadowing its own ENV declarations (CMD now reads them via shell-form ${VAR:-default}); and the P0.A Important finding that the README's Python-source setup told users to copy .env.example to .env before running doctor/serve, while .env was never actually read outside Docker Compose. OPENALPHA_LOG_LEVEL stays declared in .env.example, explicitly marked reserved for structured logging (V2-P0B-007), not wired to an unused config field.
notes: pydantic-settings is the one new runtime dependency (7 -> 8), justified and recorded in docs/architecture/ADR-0004-config-and-dotenv-loading.md. Amendment (2026-08-07, same ADR): a follow-up review found the original hand-written .env parser (config.py#_parse_dotenv_text) had two real bugs -- KEY=value # comment silently kept the trailing comment as part of the value (silent credential corruption), and export-prefixed lines were silently dropped rather than handled. python-dotenv was already a mandatory transitive dependency of pydantic-settings (confirmed in uv.lock); load_dotenv() now delegates parsing to its dotenv_values(path, interpolate=False) directly (interpolation explicitly disabled to keep this project's original no-interpolation behavior -- a credential containing a literal ${...} must survive verbatim), and python-dotenv is now declared as an explicit direct runtime dependency (python-dotenv>=1.1,<2) rather than left as an unstated transitive consequence -- runtime dependency count moves 8 -> 9, a second deliberate, recorded exception. Its default logging warning for an unparseable line (via the dotenv.main logger, independent of the verbose argument) is routed to a NullHandler with propagation disabled so a malformed .env line still degrades silently, never a crash, and never new unannounced stderr output. New regression tests cover every awkward-input case: quoted values, a hash inside quotes, an embedded = in the value, CRLF line endings, an export prefix, duplicate keys (last wins), and the no-interpolation guarantee. Separately, tests/unit/test_config.py's autouse _isolated_environ fixture previously cleared only the five OPENALPHA_* variable names, hardcoded in the test file -- it did not clear credential variables, so a shell that had exported e.g. TUSHARE_TOKEN (exactly what this repository's own root .env header comment recommends via `set -a; source .env; set +a`) leaked into every test in the file and broke three real-env-wins precedence assertions reproducibly. The fixture now derives its full clear-list directly from .env.example's declared variable names instead of a second, hand-maintained list that can drift; proven stable by re-running the full suite with seven credential variables exported as bogus values (251 passed, unchanged). Test isolation from a developer's real root .env remains structural, not best-effort, and the CLI-only load_dotenv() call boundary, discover_dotenv()'s cwd-based resolution, and the --host/--port > env/.env > default precedence are all unchanged and re-verified after this amendment -- see the P0.B task report for exact commands and output.

feature_name: Structured JSON-lines logging, library-safe by default
feature_description: Add stdlib-only structured (JSON-lines) logging, configured exclusively by this package's two real entry points -- cli.py#main and api/app.py#create_app -- never at import time and never via logging.basicConfig() (which would hijack a host process's own root-logger configuration when this package is embedded as a library via OpenAlphaSDK). Every module inside the package logs with a plain logging.getLogger(__name__) and nothing else; logging_setup.configure_logging(level) attaches one JsonLinesFormatter-formatted StreamHandler to the package's own logger namespace (openalpha_cn), idempotently (a second call, even with a different level, is a no-op, so create_app() running more than once per process -- every test that builds its own instance does -- never stacks a second handler). A permanent, inert NullHandler is attached to that namespace at import time (mirroring config.py's pre-existing dotenv.main precedent) so a WARNING+ record logged before either entry point configures anything -- e.g. _probe_report() invoked through the bare Typer app object the way CliRunner drives it in every test in this repository -- never falls through to Python's 'handler of last resort' and prints directly to real stderr, bypassing whatever stream a test harness thinks it is capturing. OPENALPHA_LOG_LEVEL (declared but unwired since Task 14) is now a real OpenAlphaConfig field, case-insensitive, restricted to DEBUG/INFO/WARNING/ERROR/CRITICAL, raising ConfigError naming OPENALPHA_LOG_LEVEL on an unknown value -- main() now eagerly calls load_config() once at startup for this (a minor, deliberate behavior tightening: any invalid OPENALPHA_* value now fails every CLI command immediately with a named error, not only the command that happens to use that field, exactly mirroring the existing serve()/ConfigError pattern). Exactly four call sites are instrumented, matching the task brief's explicit, restrained list -- no per-item or per-agent-call logging, which would bury a scheduled job's failure signal in hot-path noise: (1) cli.py#_probe_report's ProviderFailure branch logs provider_probe_failed with category/provider_id/dataset, never ProviderFailure.message (which can carry a credential or URL query string -- the exact class of leak Task 3 already shipped once, via this same function's now-adjacent generic-exception branch, which stays deliberately unlogged); (2) storage/migrations.py#run_migrations logs migration_backup_created, migration_applied per version, and migration_failed (version/name/backup_path only, never str(the underlying exception), since apply() is arbitrary caller code that could raise anything); (3) runtime/batch.py's BatchResearchService (submit/run/cancel/finish) and storage/batch.py's SQLiteBatchTaskStore.recover_interrupted log the batch lifecycle -- submitted, run_started (with a retry=True/False field derived from the task's prior failed/partial status, since run() has no separate retry entry point), cancel_requested, finished, and recovered -- deliberately never per research item (BatchTaskStore.append_event already durably records item-level outcomes through an unrelated mechanism, and a failed item's exception could carry the same class of secret ProviderFailure's message can); (4) runtime/composition.py#build_storage logs storage_initialized with runtime_dir and the resulting schema_version, once per process/runtime_dir assembly. Sentinel-driven leak proofs exercise all four: a caplog-based unit test and an end-to-end subprocess test (cli.main() actually configuring a real StreamHandler against real stderr) both drive a secret through the ProviderFailure path and assert it never appears in any captured log output; a migration test injects a RuntimeError whose message embeds a fake connection-string credential; a batch test injects a runner that always raises with an embedded secret. A shared, autouse tests/conftest.py fixture resets the openalpha_cn logger to its unconfigured default before and after every test, so uv run pytest -q's clean output and each test's log assertions are both structural guarantees rather than accidents of test execution order. Review-fix round (P0.B, three Important findings closed together, task-15-report.md): (1) JsonLinesFormatter had no whitelist -- a reviewer proved extra={"error": some_exception}, extra={"config": {...}}, and extra={"url": "...?token=..."} would all leak, even though today's 10 call sites are clean. The formatter now enforces two independent bars on every extra= field -- name must be in a new _ALLOWED_EXTRA_FIELDS inventory (required because the url case is an ordinary str, so a type-only check would miss it) and value must be a plain scalar (_SCALAR_EXTRA_TYPES, catching a future call site that reuses an allowed name for the wrong value shape) -- and a dropped field's name (never its value) is recorded under _dropped_fields in the same JSON line, so blocking is visible, not silent. (2) cli.py#main's eager load_config() before dispatch (added by this same task) validated the whole OpenAlphaConfig atomically, so one malformed OPENALPHA_* field aborted every command, including doctor (the diagnostic tool, whose entire job is diagnosing exactly that) and version (unrelated to config). main() now resolves only OPENALPHA_LOG_LEVEL via the new load_log_level(), so an invalid OPENALPHA_LOG_LEVEL itself still aborts loudly (unchanged -- guards against a scheduled job's logs going silently misconfigured) while an unrelated invalid field no longer touches dispatch at all; doctor() now calls load_config() itself and reports a ConfigError as an ordinary "config" finding in both --json and human output, with doctor --json always emitting valid JSON. (3) The permanent NullHandler was only installed as a side effect of importing logging_setup, which only cli.py and api/app.py did -- a reviewer proved a library embedder importing only openalpha_cn.sdk got no NullHandler at all, and a real migration_failed log record from storage/migrations.py printed a bare unformatted line straight to the host process's real stderr. openalpha_cn/__init__.py now imports logging_setup for this side effect, guaranteed to run for any use of the package (Python always executes a package's __init__.py before any of its submodules).
notes: test_main_entrypoint_logs_provider_probe_failure_without_leaking_the_failure_message is the acceptance test because it is the strongest available proof: unlike a caplog-based unit test, it runs cli.main() -- the real console-script entry point -- in a fresh subprocess with a provider whose fetch() raises ProviderFailure carrying a unique sentinel in its message, and asserts the sentinel appears in neither stdout nor stderr while the structured provider_probe_failed JSON log line (category/provider_id/dataset) does appear on stderr, proving the real, fully-configured logging path is safe end to end, not just the unit-tested formatter/call-site logic in isolation. Companion caplog-based tests exist per call site: test_probe_report_logs_provider_failure_category_and_provider_id_not_the_message (tests/unit/test_cli.py), test_run_migrations_logs_failure_without_leaking_the_underlying_exception_message (tests/integration/storage/test_migrations.py), test_batch_lifecycle_logs_never_leak_a_failed_items_exception_message (tests/integration/test_batch_research.py). Confirmed RED before logging_setup.py existed (ModuleNotFoundError) and RED again, per call site, before each logger.* call was added (caplog assertion failures: 'expected the ProviderFailure branch to emit a structured log line', etc.); GREEN after. 277 tests pass (251 pre-existing plus 26 new), uv run mypy src scripts / ruff check / ruff format --check / lint-imports (4 kept, 0 broken) are all clean, and coverage is 88.83%, above the 80% floor. Runtime dependency count is unchanged at nine: only the stdlib logging/json modules are used. P0.B review-fix round verification: strict TDD per finding, all three RED before their fix (formatter leak tests failed with the secret literally present in the JSON line; the doctor/main tests failed with json.JSONDecodeError on empty stdout and version exiting non-zero; the SDK backstop tests failed with handlers == [] and a bare 'migration_failed' line on real stderr) and GREEN after. New/updated tests: tests/unit/test_logging_setup.py (6 new: 4 leak-experiment reproductions plus the visible-evidence and positive-control tests), tests/unit/test_config.py (5 new, load_log_level), tests/unit/test_cli.py (6 new: 3 CliRunner-level doctor config-finding tests, 3 subprocess-level main() tests), and a new file tests/unit/test_sdk_logging_backstop.py (2 subprocess-isolated tests, mirroring test_contracts_import_isolation.py's style -- the second probe reproduces a genuine sqlite3.OperationalError by pre-creating a runs table with an archived_at column under a different case, not an injected fake migration). No existing test's assertions were modified; 296 tests pass (277 pre-existing plus 19 new), uv run mypy src scripts / ruff check / ruff format --check / lint-imports (4 kept, 0 broken) are all clean, and coverage is 88.96%, above the 80% floor. Runtime dependency count is unchanged at nine.

feature_name: Real code-commit/config-digest provenance and a random-seed seeding mechanism
feature_description: Replace three placeholder provenance inputs that fed decision_id's content-addressed hash with real values. code_commit: cli.py's --code-commit used to default to the literal string "development" (client.ts sent "web-development"); runtime/provenance.py#resolve_code_commit now resolves, in order, a live git workspace (git rev-parse HEAD anchored at this module's own installed location, never the process cwd, with a literal -dirty suffix appended whenever `git status --porcelain --untracked-files=normal` reports any staged, unstaged, or untracked-and-not-ignored change), a build-time-embedded stamp (_build_commit.py#BUILD_COMMIT, unpopulated until a release pipeline exists but fully implemented and tested), or an explicit UNKNOWN_CODE_COMMIT marker ("unknown-not-a-git-commit") that can never be mistaken for a real hex SHA. config_digest: cli.py used to default to "0" * 64; runtime/provenance.py#compute_config_digest now returns a real SHA-256 over an explicit allow-list of OpenAlphaConfig's own fields (runtime_dir, web_dir, max_request_bytes, host, port, log_level) -- the entire configuration surface this package has today -- deliberately excluding every provider/model credential, which never enters OpenAlphaConfig in the first place (config.py's own module docstring), so there is nothing to filter at digest time and no dictionary-attack surface from publishing two manifests. random_seed: carried through every layer since ResearchRunRequest existed but never read to seed anything; runtime/seeding.py adds a small pluggable registry (register_random_source/seed_everything) that stdlib random joins unconditionally and numpy.random joins only when numpy is importable (guarded, since numpy is not a runtime dependency yet per ADR-0003) -- ResearchEngine.run_cycle calls seed_everything(request.random_seed) once, at the same deterministic boundary every other per-run input is threaded through. No production component consumes the seeded state yet (the baseline agents are deterministic arithmetic, and backtest/event_study.py's own bootstrap seeds from its own separate EventStudyRequest.random_seed via a local random.Random instance, untouched by this module's global random.seed() call) -- this task builds and proves the mechanism, honestly, not a fabricated consumer. seed_everything also pins every BLAS/OpenMP thread-count env var ADR-0003 names (OMP_NUM_THREADS, OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS, MKL_NUM_THREADS, VECLIB_MAXIMUM_THREADS, NUMEXPR_NUM_THREADS) to "1" and sets PYTHONHASHSEED (for subprocesses/workers spawned afterward, since CPython cannot change hash randomization for its own already-running interpreter); the Dockerfile pins the same five BLAS env vars at container start, ahead of the numerical stack that does not exist yet, so P4 does not have to remember to add either. Critical review follow-up: the web UI (`web/src/api/client.ts`) POSTed the fabricated literals `code_commit: "web-development"` and `config_digest: "0".repeat(64)` on every `/api/v1/research/run`/`/api/v1/backtests/replay` call, because `ResearchApiRequest`/`ReplayApiRequest` (api/app.py) required both fields with no server-side fallback -- so the web UI was the only remaining source of fabricated provenance. A `model_validator(mode="before")` shared by both request models (`_fill_missing_provenance`, backed by the same `_resolved_code_commit`/`_resolved_config_digest` pattern cli.py already uses) now resolves both fields server-side whenever a caller omits them, and honours an explicitly supplied value verbatim otherwise (preserving REST/SDK parity, test_rest_sdk_clock_parity.py). client.ts no longer sends either literal.
notes: Acceptance test runs the real CLI end to end with --code-commit/--config-digest omitted and asserts the resulting manifest's code_commit is neither "development" nor the unknown marker (this test runs inside a real git checkout) and is a 40-hex-character SHA (optionally -dirty-suffixed), and config_digest is a real 64-hex-character SHA-256, never "0" * 64. test_cli_replay.py's two tests intercept ReplayRunner.__init__ (the sole construction point sdk.py#OpenAlphaSDK.replay reaches) to prove replay run's defaults resolve the same way, and that explicit --code-commit/--config-digest flags still pass through verbatim -- ReplayReport carries no code_commit/config_digest field of its own to assert on directly. test_provenance.py proves all three resolve_code_commit tiers against real git subprocesses in an isolated tmp_path repo (clean HEAD, -dirty for uncommitted changes, -dirty for a new untracked file), the hard "must work outside a git repository" requirement with a tmp_path that has no .git in any parent, a FileNotFoundError-simulating monkeypatch for the "git binary not installed" wheel-install case, the build-embedded-stamp tier via monkeypatching _build_commit.BUILD_COMMIT, and an explicit assertion that the unknown marker is not lowercase-hex-only (so it can never be confused with a real SHA) and is not the string "development". compute_config_digest is proven deterministic, sensitive to a real config change, and -- the task's named trap -- provably unaffected by an unrelated credential env var (TUSHARE_TOKEN) being set. test_seeding.py proves the registry is generic (a test-registered fake source receives the seed exactly like the real ones), that stdlib random is genuinely reseeded (same seed -> same 5-draw Dockerfile BLAS/OpenMP env vars by literal substring. All pre-existing 299 tests still pass unmodified: every one that constructs ResearchRunRequest/RunManifest/DecisionLedger already passes an explicit code_commit (typically "0123456789abcdef") and config_digest, so none depended on the old cli.py placeholder defaults; only cli.py's own two Typer commands changed default behavior, and neither had a pre-existing test pinning the old defaults. uv run mypy src scripts / ruff check / ruff format --check / lint-imports (4 kept, 0 broken) are all clean; coverage is 89.16%, above the 80% floor. feature_name: Durable outcome-validation ledger with an SDK entry point
feature_description: Persist ValidationResult in an append-only, content-addressed-idempotent SQLite ledger created by a schema migration (not a constructor side effect), indexed on decision_id and signal_id, queryable from both REST and the SDK; add the SDK's own OutcomeValidator entry point so a programmatic caller can validate and persist an outcome without going through HTTP.
notes: V2-P0B-010 (audit F67, F29). Before this task POST /api/v1/backtests/validate computed a ValidationResult and discarded it, and sdk.py never imported backtest.validation at all, so a past decision's outcome could never be looked back up and a programmatic caller had no way to validate one without HTTP. Append is idempotent by validation_id (content-derived) and rejects a differing payload under a reused ID -- proven in test_validation_store.py::test_append_is_idempotent_for_the_identical_result and ::test_append_rejects_a_conflicting_reuse_of_the_same_validation_id (the latter hand-inserts a mismatched row via sqlite3 directly, since a real hash collision cannot be constructed from two honestly-computed results). Both query paths (decision_id, signal_id) get their own index (validation_results_decision_id_idx, validation_results_signal_id_idx), so this table does not become project audit finding F69's fourth full-scan case. The create_validation_results migration is deliberately ordered *before* the pre-existing demo_add_runs_archived_at migration (bumped from version 2 to version 3): both are precondition-free, but the executor stops applying migrations the moment one defers, and the demo migration always defers on a brand-new database (it alters runs, which SQLiteRunRepository's constructor -- not yet invoked -- creates); ordered after it instead, this table would never be created within the very first build_storage() call on a fresh install, leaving every validate call broken until a process restart. This ordering interaction is the subtlety task-18-brief.md flagged and asked to be confirmed rather than assumed; confirming it empirically (by adding the migration and running the full suite) surfaced 13 pre-existing tests whose hardcoded schema-version expectations legitimately shifted by the registry's growth -- all updated using symbolic constants or a computed doomed_version instead of new hardcoded literals where possible, documented in task-18-report.md.

feature_name: Partitioned panel store skeleton with a persistent DuckDB catalog
feature_description: `dataset/year/`-partitioned Parquet storage for ADR-0002's panel data plane -- write_partition()'s overwrite-per-partition idempotency, query()/profile_query()'s catalog-driven single-partition resolution (never a directory glob), and structural proof of partition pruning and column projection via DuckDB's own profiling output, kept fully separate from ParquetEvidenceStore and free of numpy/pandas and pydantic on the read path.
notes: V2-P1-001 (audit F16, F71-F75, F84; PRD S91, Implementation Decision 31). Builds the panel data plane's storage skeleton ADR-0002 calls for, without touching ParquetEvidenceStore or ingesting any real dataset (V2-P1-002/003/004+ remain separate, later tasks). Partition granularity is dataset/year/, one Parquet file per partition, written through the same temp-then-atomic-rename idiom ParquetEvidenceStore.append already uses. The persistent catalog.duckdb file holds only a small panel_partitions metadata table (never the panel data itself); query()/profile_query() resolve (dataset, year) to a single explicit file path via an indexed catalog lookup -- never Path.glob()/Path.rglob() (proven by test_panel_store_read_path_never_globs_the_dataset_directory's AST assertion) -- so partition pruning is a structural guarantee, not an optimizer hope. Partition pruning and column projection are proven via DuckDB's own PRAGMA-profiling JSON output (Total Files Read, Filename(s), Projections, total_bytes_read), never wall-clock timing. Zero pydantic construction on the read path is an AST assertion (the whole module never imports pydantic); zero SHA-256 on the read path is a call-count spy on hashlib.sha256, separately proving the write path does hash (idempotency) so the zero-count on query()/profile_query() is meaningful, not vacuous. Dependency decision: no numpy/pandas -- DuckDB's own relational API (execute/executemany/COPY TO PARQUET/read_parquet) fully covers partitioned write, column projection, and pruning for this skeleton, at zero additional runtime-dependency cost and without triggering ADR-0003's mypy-strict follow_imports=skip + warn_return_any chain reaction. openalpha_cn.panel is a new top-level sibling package with zero openalpha_cn.* imports of its own (fully self-contained on DuckDB + stdlib), and neither storage nor domain import it -- both directions proven with grimp in test_import_layering.py (test_panel_package_has_zero_direct_edges_into_any_other_openalpha_cn_subpackage, test_storage_and_domain_have_zero_direct_edges_into_the_new_panel_package); domain-purity's existing dynamic sibling-subpackage discovery already covered the domain->panel direction with zero edits. A real bug surfaced during development: PanelStore.__init__ originally opened the catalog read-write unconditionally to run CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS, so three concurrent reader processes in test_concurrent_read_only_queries_from_separate_processes_do_not_fail_each_other raced for the exclusive lock and crashed with duckdb.IOException; fixed by making construction side-effect-free and creating the schema lazily inside write_partition()'s own read-write transaction. See task-24-report.md for full storage-layout, concurrency, and EXPLAIN/profiling evidence. Follow-up review (task 24) closed three findings without touching ParquetEvidenceStore or wiring panel/ into anything: (1) dataset was unvalidated, so write_partition() and profile_query() could be pointed outside root by a relative traversal (dataset="../escaped") or an absolute path (Path(root) / dataset discards root, pathlib's documented behavior for an absolute right operand) -- both reproduced as real files written outside root before the fix; a shared _validate_dataset() now runs at the top of all three public methods. (2) profile_query()'s profiling-output filename had no per-call uniqueness, contradicting the module docstring's concurrent-readers claim -- 8 concurrent same-process threads against the same partition produced 3-6 failures per run across 5 runs (FileNotFoundError or JSONDecodeError); fixed with a uuid4-suffixed filename per call. (3) the documented concurrent-write failure mode (duckdb.IOException) was only ever tested across OS processes; this codebase's actual concurrency primitive is runtime/batch.py's ThreadPoolExecutor (same-process threads), which pre-fix hit duckdb.TransactionException: Catalog write-write conflict (4 threads, 4 different datasets, cold start, 3 of 4 failing reproducibly) and a raw FileNotFoundError from a shared, non-unique write_partition() temp filename (same partition, same-process threads). Fixed with a per-writer-unique temp filename (removes the FileNotFoundError) and an in-process threading.Lock serializing only write_partition()'s few-millisecond catalog upsert (removes the TransactionException); cross-process writer races remain a documented, deliberately out-of-scope limitation a threading.Lock cannot address. Two design characteristics recorded, not fixed: no range query (year is a mandatory single int; a multi-year read needs caller-side looping over query()) and no row-group pruning within a partition (an equality filter narrows the result set DuckDB returns, not the row groups it scans). See tests/integration/panel/test_panel_store_hardening.py and task-24-report.md's follow-up section for the full reproduction and fix evidence.

feature_name: Columnar provider batch contract for the panel plane
feature_description: ColumnarPanelBatch, the column-oriented sibling of providers/base.py's row-wise ProviderBatch, for ADR-0002's panel data plane. Same four-clock point-in-time guarantee (proven equivalent to ProviderBatch.validate_result's per-record is_visible_at scan by running both contracts over the same corpus, including 200 randomised cases and the exact as_of boundary), same explicit success/no_data semantics, but per-row content addressing (ProviderRecord.record_id) is replaced by a single batch-level content_digest computed once at construction rather than on every access. Measured at 1.80 us/row against the row-wise path's 13.9 us/row for identical source data (2,000 rows x 5 float fields), a 7.8x reduction; the same re-measurement is quoted in domain/panel_batch.py and in tests/contract/panel/test_columnar_batch_parity.py, which an earlier version of this row contradicted (1.68 us/row, 8.2x). The wall-clock assertion is only a backstop at 6x: each cost claim also has an exact, load-independent structural assertion (serialization count for the digest, is_visible_at call count for the point-in-time check, transpose count for to_rows), because a 4x threshold demonstrably passed implementations that had reverted to per-row work. panel_ingest.write_panel_batch feeds a batch to PanelStore.write_partition without per-row unpacking (one C-level zip transpose). Column names, column kinds and the dataset name are validated at the contract boundary AND re-validated for every caller-supplied column in _check_shape, and panel/store.py escapes every SQL identifier it interpolates while accepting column types only from a closed set.
notes: V2-P1-002 (audit F15, F75; PRD S91, Implementation Decision 32). Coexists with ProviderBatch/ProviderRecord rather than replacing them -- the evidence plane keeps per-row content addressing, which ADR-0002 identifies as a correctness feature there and a wall at panel scale (1.35e7 rows/field). What the batch-level digest does NOT provide is stated explicitly: a corrupted batch is detectable but the digest cannot name the offending row, and no row can be looked up by content. The digest covers the batch header plus every storage column with its name, kind and length; timestamps are normalised to UTC and hashed as integer microseconds, which is what lets the digest survive a real Parquet+DuckDB round trip (DuckDB returns TIMESTAMPTZ in the session timezone, not UTC). Plain frozen dataclasses, not pydantic, following panel/store.py's ColumnSpec precedent: pydantic validates per element, which is the cost this contract exists to remove. The contract lives in domain/ so providers/ can produce it and panel_ingest can consume it without a providers<->panel edge; the seam is a neutral top-level module rather than panel/ingest.py because V2-P1-001 pinned openalpha_cn.panel as importing no sibling subpackage at all -- the same response batch_contracts.py embodies in V2-P0B-012, though not the same direction (batch_contracts sits below the packages it decouples, this sits above), and not the only available shape (a panel-side Protocol with injection would also satisfy the rule; it is deferred until the seam has more than one caller). CORRECTION to this row's first version, which claimed column names 'cannot reach PanelStore's interpolated SQL': they could. ColumnarPanelBatch.columns is an ordinary tuple field, so a column object that never ran PanelColumn.__post_init__ carried a hostile name into write_partition's CREATE TABLE DDL and executed the ATTACH inside it. Closed on both sides now -- _check_shape re-validates name and kind per column, and store.py escapes identifiers and closes its type set -- with the three store-level injections (unquoted duckdb_type, SELECT projection, WHERE key) covered by tests/integration/panel/test_panel_store_hardening.py. Open follow-ups, recorded rather than fixed: content_digest is never persisted, so a partition on disk cannot later be re-proved against the digest its batch carried (belongs with V2-P1-003's data catalog); and no src/ caller invokes write_panel_batch yet -- the first arrives with V2-P1-004. No dataset is wired up (V2-P1-004+) and no data catalog is built (V2-P1-003); numpy/pandas stay out per ADR-0003 and the runtime dependency set is unchanged at 9.

feature_name: Panel data catalog and readiness contract
feature_description: The catalog half of PRD Story S8 plus the readiness contract V2-P1-012/013/016 are built on. V2-P1-001's panel_partitions answered one of S8's five questions (where the file is, how many rows, its storage hash, when it landed) and none of subjects / fields / date coverage / revision coverage / freshness. Six additive tables now answer all five: panel_partition_coverage (provenance, freshness, counts), plus the subject, field, date and revision censuses, keyed on (dataset, year) exactly as panel_partitions is. panel_partitions itself is untouched, so partitions written before this task need no migration -- they simply have no coverage row, a state readiness reports as coverage_missing rather than mistaking for health. Freshness is measured on the event clock (last_event_time, how far the data reaches), never on the write clock, because a backfill run today can produce a partition whose newest event is a month old. Revision coverage carries two facets because one provably cannot see the case that motivates it: roadmap section 7 measured that Tushare restatements share both announcement dates and differ only in update_flag, so the clock-derived revised_row_count reads 0 on exactly that data while the opaque label census sees both versions. The readiness contract is fail-closed and as_of-relative: unknown coverage blocks, a requirement naming no year blocks, staleness is as_of minus last_event_time, and a partition whose newest available_time post-dates as_of is refused as not_yet_knowable. read_if_ready() makes blocked and empty two different values (rows_or_none is None versus ()), which query() alone cannot express, and its plainly-named rows accessor raises on a blocked outcome so the truthiness that would re-merge them cannot pass quietly.
notes: V2-P1-003 (PRD S8, Implementation Decision 5; consumed by V2-P1-012 health report, V2-P1-013 fail-closed gate, V2-P1-016 REST/SDK surface). Two catalog judgements are recorded rather than assumed. First, both hashes are kept: PanelStore.content_hash covers (dataset, year, column names and SQL types, rows) and makes a re-write of identical content a true no-op, while ColumnarPanelBatch.content_digest additionally covers provider_id/kind/as_of/fetched_at/source_uri/schema_version and lets a later reader re-prove provenance; substituting the digest for the hash would rewrite an unchanged partition on every refetch (fetched_at is hashed into it), and substituting the hash for the digest would lose the fetch -- closing the m3 gap V2-P1-002 recorded without collapsing two different questions into one number. Second, DuckDB's now() in write_partition was replaced by an injected clock (default datetime.now(UTC), naive clocks refused): it was a bare wall-clock read inside the database that no test could freeze, and a readiness contract asserting on catalog timestamps needs them reproducible. panel/catalog.py's dataclasses deliberately carry no validating __post_init__ -- the rule lives once, at PanelStore.record_coverage, because V2-P1-002's review proved a nominal type is not a boundary. Catalog schema evolution is the panel plane's own concern, not storage/migrations.py's (that engine is SQLite PRAGMA user_version and cannot govern a DuckDB file): the catalog stamps panel-catalog/v1 and refuses an unknown newer stamp. No dataset is ingested (V2-P1-004+), no trading calendar exists yet so date holes are detected against caller-supplied required_dates, numpy/pandas stay out per ADR-0003, and the runtime dependency set is unchanged at 9. Follow-up review (task 26) closed one Critical and three interface findings, all reproduced against a1939cc before the fix. (C1) A coverage record was bound to the partition it describes only at the instant record_coverage ran, so any later write_partition for the same (dataset, year) -- a backfill or a correction, precisely what overwrite-per-partition semantics exist for -- left the catalog describing content that was no longer on disk while readiness returned state=ready issues=[] under the strictest possible requirement; the interrupted-ingest case (write_partition succeeded, record_coverage did not) therefore failed *open* on every re-write, contradicting the module docstring's fail-closed claim, which was true of first writes only. Fixed by recording panel_partition_coverage.partition_content_hash and blocking on coverage_stale whenever it differs from the partition's current hash or is unknown -- a row count cannot see this, because a correction that restates values leaves the count identical and moves the hash. (I1) ReadinessRequirement's four checks defaulted to their most permissive values, so a default-constructed requirement never emitted date_gap (empty set difference) or stale (no bound), and a 2024 partition holding one trading day was ready on 2024-12-31; the defaults are gone, None waives a check and is recorded in DatasetReadiness.checks_waived for V2-P1-012/013 to see, and a declared-but-empty tuple blocks with empty_requirement -- the same rule no_years_requested already applied to years. (I3) PanelReadOutcome.rows was tuple | None, which mypy strict cannot stop `if not outcome.rows:` or `outcome.rows or []` from silently merging blocked with ready-and-empty at run time; the field is now rows_or_none and rows is a property that raises PanelStorageError on a blocked outcome, chosen over a sealed ReadyRead|BlockedRead union because it costs no new types and no narrowing at every consumer while making the same wrong lines fail loudly. (I2) The schema stamp guarded three of six public methods; query() -- the only one that reads panel_partitions.relative_path and opens the file it names -- returned rows from a v99 catalog. It now guards all six. (I4) Path.is_file() called a zero-byte partition ready and read_if_ready leaked a bare duckdb.InvalidInputException; readiness now checks Parquet's own magic at both ends (partition_file_unreadable) and read_if_ready wraps any scan failure as PanelStorageError -- a file replaced by a different but valid Parquet is still out of reach of an O(1) check and is left to V2-P1-012's deep pass. Minors: the date census must now fall inside the partition's own year (a 2019 batch written with year=2024 was ready); _validated_requirement checks container types so years=None names itself instead of raising TypeError from inside the validator; the version check moved ahead of the DDL pass, which had been rebuilding five dropped tables before the refusal fired; and coverage timestamps are normalised to UTC on read-back rather than carrying the DuckDB session's local offset onto V2-P1-016's wire. The catalog stamp moved to panel-catalog/v2 with a real forward ALTER TABLE migration: partition_content_hash is structurally additive, but a v1 build reading a v2 catalog would ignore it and report ready for exactly the stale-coverage partitions a v2 build blocks, which is the silent fail-open the stamp exists to prevent, so v1 readers are refused; this build still reads a v1 catalog, with the unknown hash treated as coverage_stale until one record_coverage call migrates and re-stamps it. Not a DROP and re-derive, because provider_id/as_of/fetched_at/batch_digest exist nowhere but this catalog.

feature_name: Real exchange trading calendar with a three-valued verdict
feature_description: Tushare's trade_cal wired onto the descriptor table as V2-P1-004's dataset (1), plus the TradingCalendar contract every downstream time alignment reads. Replaces the only calendar the repository had, scripts/generate_replay_corpus.py's weekday() < 5 (audit F49). A live probe of the published SSE series -- 13,162 rows, 1990-12-19 through 2026-12-31 -- measured what that approximation costs: 605 closed weekdays and zero open weekends, so the error is one-directional and never crashes anything downstream. The verdict is three-valued because a boolean answer conflates 'the exchange was shut' with 'the exchange has not published that far': the same probe returns zero rows for all of 2027, so a boolean calendar reads the whole year as one continuous holiday. CalendarDayStatus is trading / closed / beyond_horizon and raises on bool(), is_trading_day() raises CalendarHorizonError instead of answering False outside the horizon, and trading_days_between / next_trading_day / previous_trading_day / shift all refuse rather than truncate. build_trading_calendar applies the same rule one range narrower, refusing a set of days with a hole in it so the horizon describes the whole interval and not just its endpoints. The calendar is stored on ADR-0002's panel plane through TushareProvider.fetch_panel (the first PanelDataProvider implementation and the first src/ caller of write_panel_batch), and panel_readiness_requirement turns it back into the required_dates V2-P1-003 had to leave caller-supplied.
notes: V2-P1-004 (audit F49; PRD S12; roadmap section 6 dataset 1; depended on by V2-P1-005/006/011/012/017). Four design judgements are recorded rather than assumed, each measured against the live endpoint. (1) available_time is min(start of the calendar date's own year, the moment the row was observed), and taking a minimum rather than picking one bound is the whole rule. The first bound needs no guess about when the exchange published -- by the time year Y has begun, year Y's calendar certainly exists -- and it is what makes 2026-12-31 visible at as_of=2026-08-08 (availability 2026-01-01) while 2027-01-04 is not (availability 2027-01-01). The second bound exists because Tushare publishes next year's calendar during December: without it, Timeline would refuse a 2027 row fetched in 2026-12 for having been ingested before it was available, which contradicts the fact that we demonstrably had it. Both bounds are facts this code holds, and the conservative choice is the largest instant neither contradicts. The cost is real and deliberate: between the exchange's November announcement and 1 January the rule blocks questions about the coming year that were in fact answerable -- it errs toward refusing, which is the direction a point-in-time system is allowed to be wrong in. ClockStrategy.calendar_static was NOT reused: it sets available_time to the row's own midnight, which would hide every future session from every earlier as_of, the exact defect this dataset exists to remove. It keeps its synthetic tests and still has no production consumer. (2) The three-valued verdict is guarded twice, because two values alone are re-merged by Python's truthiness -- the failure mode V2-P1-003's PanelReadOutcome.rows already answered for. CalendarDayStatus.__bool__ raises for EVERY member, not only beyond_horizon: making two of three usable as conditions and the third explosive is a landmine, not a guardrail. is_trading_day() then keeps a plain bool return but raises outside the horizon, so `if not calendar.is_trading_day(day):` -- the way people actually write this -- cannot receive the unknown case at all. (3) pretrade_date is stored but never trusted as the answer. previous_trading_day is derived from the session sequence and the column is kept as an independent witness; the live probe found 0 disagreements across all 13,162 rows and the tests re-prove it on the fixtures. The recorded cost: pretrade_date on the first row of a window names a session before the horizon, and previous_trading_day(horizon.first_date) raises rather than using it, because a horizon whose meaning depends on which end you ask from is not a horizon. (4) scripts/generate_replay_corpus.py's weekday() < 5 was deliberately NOT changed, and the reasoning is recorded in that script's own docstring. Its dates are synthetic case identities (source_uri=fixture://replay/NNN), not claims about the exchange; run_id is derived from the date, so a different day set would rewrite all 300 ids and every artifact keyed by them; the real 2026 calendar closes 2026-02-14..2026-02-23 inside that window, so the change would be far from cosmetic while making the 300/300/0 determinism assertion no stronger; and using the calendar there would put either a network call or a maintained calendar fixture into the one script whose purpose is determinism. F49's actual finding -- that the approximation was the only calendar in the repository -- is closed either way. V2-P4-022 replaces that corpus outright. Storage and layering: the contract lives in domain/ (pure datetime + bisect + dataclasses), so providers/ can produce it and panel_ingest can read it back without a providers<->panel edge; TRADING_CALENDAR_DATASET and the column names live there too because panel_ingest is pinned to importing domain and panel only. openalpha_cn.panel still imports no sibling subpackage and lint-imports remains 4 kept / 0 broken. is_open is parsed, never coerced: bool('0') is True, so _open_flag accepts only 0/1/'0'/'1'/bool and the read-back path re-checks the type, because a truthy stand-in would turn every holiday into a session. fetch_panel distinguishes two empty results -- zero rows served (an unpublished horizon) from rows served but none knowable at as_of -- and sorts Tushare's descending response ascending so a partition's content hash does not depend on an upstream ordering. panel_partition_year derives the partition key from the batch's own event census in the declared timezone and refuses a batch spanning two years, closing the gap panel_ingest.py recorded; resolving in UTC instead is proven to misfile the 2024-01-01 session, which is 2023-12-31 in UTC. trading_calendar_requirement waives required_dates (stating it would be circular; build_trading_calendar's contiguity rule is strictly stronger) and max_staleness (a calendar's newest event is in the future, so as_of - last_event_time is negative and the check can never fire -- a check that cannot fail reads as reassurance), and both waivers land in DatasetReadiness.checks_waived rather than being invisible.
